title: The overview effect
hook: Many astronauts say seeing Earth from space changed how they think about home.
peek: Many astronauts describe a sudden shift on seeing Earth hanging in space: borders vanish, the atmosphere looks paper thin, and home feels fragile. A writer named it the overview effect in 1987.
lede: Astronauts often come back describing something the training did not cover. Seeing the whole planet hanging in black space, with no borders visible and an atmosphere that looks thin as a skin, many report a lasting sense that Earth is small, fragile and shared. In 1987 the writer Frank White gave it a name in his book The Overview Effect.

bullets.text: On 24 December 1968, Apollo 8 astronaut Bill Anders photographed Earth rising over the Moon's horizon. The picture became one of the most famous ever taken.
In 1990 Voyager 1 looked back from about six billion kilometres and caught Earth as a single faint pixel. Carl Sagan made it a lesson in humility.
From orbit, most borders are invisible. On the ground, some are odd enough that one patch of desert between Egypt and Sudan is claimed by no country at all.
Many astronauts say the atmosphere surprised them most. Seen edge-on, it looks like a thin band of blue around the planet. It is the layer that holds all the weather and air anyone has ever breathed.

Researchers have interviewed astronauts and found the shift is commonly reported and sometimes long-lasting, though it is hard to measure and not everyone feels it. Some groups now try to recreate a taste of it with virtual reality.
The Voyager probes carry a golden record of sounds and images from Earth, another attempt to see our planet as a whole.
